Induction Machines: Tests, Maximum Torque and Generator Mode (Ch7)

Why this matters in the exam: Q3(b) and Q3(c) are always Ch7 induction-machine numericals. Jun24 Q3b (4 marks) is exactly “find R1, R2’ and X from the no-load and blocked-rotor tests”. Jun24 Q3c (10 marks) runs the machine as a generator at 1025 rpm. Jun23 Q3b (5 marks) asks for the external rotor resistance that gives maximum torque at standstill, plus a torque–speed sketch. Jun23 Q3c(ii) (1 mark) is “motor or generator?”. Q4c short answers have also asked about Ch7: Jun24 4c(iii) on the no-load current (3 marks) and Jun23 4c(iii) on a perfectly conducting rotor (2 marks). That is about 15–20 marks of each paper. There are no worked solutions for Ch7 in your files, only numerical answers, so this pack gives every solution in full.

Pack M7 covered slip, the equivalent circuit, power flow and the torque formula. This pack assumes you can already do and .

1.5 External rotor resistance (wound rotor) (Lecture 7.9.1–7.9.3)

A wound rotor brings its winding out through slip rings, so you can add (referred to the stator) in series with . The effective rotor resistance becomes .

For maximum torque at standstill, set :

The starting torque then equals , and the starting current drops. Uses: (1) better starting, then remove for efficiency; (2) limited speed control of fan loads, which is inefficient because of the extra slip (ideal efficiency ).

Trap: if the question asks for the “total effective rotor resistance” (PQ 7.15(d)), the answer is . If it asks for the “external resistance” (Jun23 Q3b), subtract .

Example 2’s motor: raise R2’ from 1 Ω towards 4.12 Ω (R2’ + R2EXT’) and watch the peak slide to standstill while its height stays at about 197 Nm.

1.6 V/f (volts-per-hertz) speed control (Lecture 7.9.4–7.9.5)

An inverter changes , so it changes . Neglecting , , so to keep the peak flux at its rated value (no saturation), keep

Effects:

  • The τ–n curve keeps its shape and slides left. The slip speed for a given torque stays about the same.
  • stays constant (exactly, if is neglected), so you can get maximum torque even near standstill.
  • Operating slip stays small, so efficiency stays high over a wide speed range.

How to analyse it: use the same circuit and torque formula, but scale three things with : , (since ), and . and do not change.

Trap: at low frequency gets small, so is no longer negligible, and drops a little (New Q3 shows this).

New Q2’s motor: take f to 25 Hz and V to about 120 V together. The curve slides left, τ_max drops by about 13 % because of R1, and the slip speed at the 60 Nm load hardly changes.

1.8 Two short-answer explanations

Why the no-load current is not zero, and why it is large (Jun24 4c(iii), PQ 7.10(o)):

  • At no load the rotor runs at nearly synchronous speed, so the rotor current is almost zero. The stator still has to set up the rotating airgap flux. That needs magnetising current in . An induction machine has an airgap, so it needs much more magnetising current than a transformer. The no-load current is typically 25–60 % of rated current (Lecture 7.8.5).
  • The alternating flux causes hysteresis and eddy-current loss in the stator iron. This is modelled by and needs an in-phase current component.
  • The rotor is still turning, so friction (bearings) and windage (air drag, cooling fan) need a small mechanical power. The rotor therefore runs slightly below synchronous speed, with a small rotor current.
  • The current is mainly magnetising, so the power factor at no load is very low.

What zero rotor resistance would mean (Jun23 4c(iii), “perfectly conducting rotor”):

  • , so there are no rotor copper losses. Ideal efficiency would be higher.
  • , so the torque–speed curve near becomes vertical, like a synchronous machine.
  • Starting torque is proportional to , so it is zero. The motor could not start by itself.

2. The method

Recognise the question type first:

  • It gives test readings (V, I, P) → Type A, parameters.
  • It says “maximum torque”, “pull-out” or “speed at maximum torque” → Type B.
  • It says “external resistance”, “wound rotor” or “maximum torque at standstill” → Type C.
  • It gives a speed above , or says “run as a generator” → Type D.
  • It says “inverter”, “volts per hertz” or “frequency reduced” → Type E.

  1. Convert every reading to per-phase: (star), . The current is already per-phase for star.

4. Traps that cost marks

  • Line values in the tests. Divide by and by 3 before computing , , , . (Prac data is already per phase. Exam data is line values.)
  • Using in the blocked-rotor test. is . Use or .
  • Forgetting to subtract . The blocked-rotor test gives . needs the DC test.
  • Using or just in . It is the magnitude .
  • Using rotor speed in . is divided by . Only is divided by .
  • Thinking extra rotor resistance raises . It raises starting torque and moves the peak. The peak height does not change.
  • Dropping the minus sign in generator mode. , , , and are all negative. A positive answer for Jun24 Q3c(ii) power loses the marks. Phase angles near are correct, not an error.
  • V/f: scaling only . You must also scale and with .

New Q6 (short answer, words only) [6 marks].

  1. Carefully explain why an induction motor draws a significant current at no load, and why its power factor is low there. [3]
  2. A squirrel-cage rotor is made with zero resistance. How would this change the machine’s behaviour? [3]
Solution

  1. At no load the rotor runs at almost synchronous speed, so very little rotor current flows. The stator must still produce the rotating magnetic field. Because the flux has to cross an airgap, this needs a large magnetising current, typically a quarter to over half of rated current. That current is modelled by the magnetising reactance. A smaller in-phase current supplies the hysteresis and eddy-current losses in the stator iron, which are modelled by the core-loss resistance. A further small in-phase current supplies the friction and windage losses, because the rotor is still turning. The current is mostly magnetising current, which lags the voltage by nearly 90 degrees, so the power factor is very low.

  2. There would be no rotor copper loss, so efficiency would rise. The slip at maximum torque is proportional to rotor resistance, so it would be zero. The torque–speed curve near synchronous speed would become vertical, like a synchronous machine, and the speed would not drop with load. The starting torque is proportional to rotor resistance, so it would be zero, and the motor could not start by itself.
